bib.title: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, ch. 13 Sequential Data

question: How can sequential, non-i.i.d. data be modelled tractably with Markov models and latent-variable state space models (HMMs and linear dynamical systems), and how are inference and learning done?

results.claim: A general conditional probability table for a first-order Markov chain over K-state discrete variables has K(K-1) parameters.

limits: Stationary case only; nonstationary generative distributions are explicitly out of scope (p. 606).
HMM is a poor generative model for digits (Fig 13.11), has exponentially decaying state durations, and poor long-range correlations (pp. 631-632).
LDS linear-Gaussian assumption means observed marginal is a single Gaussian; non-Gaussian emissions make exact inference intractable (p. 644).
Factorial HMM and switching SSM have no exact tractable E step; variational or sampling approximations needed (pp. 634-635, 644).

Fully Bayesian LDS treatment omitted for lack of space (p. 644). No neural sequence models beyond brief mentions of neural emission densities and tapped delay lines; predates LSTM-era RNN/attention work.
Only experiment is a small handwritten digit demo with 45 examples; no quantitative evaluation.
practices: Use rescaled alpha/beta with scaling factors c_n rather than raw forward-backward to avoid underflow beyond ~100 steps (sec 13.2.4, p. 627).
Initialise HMM emission parameters by fitting the data as i.i.d. first, or K-means for Gaussians; initialise A and pi randomly or uniformly; zeros in A or pi stay zero under EM (pp. 617, 623).
Train on multiple shorter sequences for left-to-right models, since each off-diagonal transition occurs at most once per sequence (p. 624, Ex 13.12).
For sequence classification, train per-class HMMs discriminatively by cross-entropy (13.72) rather than maximum likelihood (p. 631).
Use Viterbi, not individually most probable states from gamma, to get the best state sequence (p. 629).
Use autoregressive HMM to capture longer-range correlations, input-output HMM for supervised sequence learning (pp. 632-633).
For LDS, use Kalman filter for real-time prediction and RTS smoother for learning parameters via EM (pp. 637-642).
Use extended Kalman filter or particle filter when dynamics or emissions are not linear-Gaussian (pp. 644-645).

terms.definition: a Markov chain in which the conditional distributions p(xn|xn-1) are constrained to be equal (stationary time series)
a Markov chain of latent variables zn with each observation xn conditioned on zn
state space model whose latent variables are discrete; equivalent to a mixture model whose component choice depends on the previous component
state space model in which both latent and observed variables are linear-Gaussian
storing the previous M observed values and using a parametric model such as a neural network to predict the next
HMM with Ajk=0 for k<j, so a vacated state cannot be re-entered
forward-backward algorithm with alpha(zn)=p(x1..xn,zn) and beta(zn)=p(xn+1..xN|zn); gamma=alpha*beta/p(X)
max-sum algorithm applied to the HMM to find the most probable state sequence
Kn = P_{n-1} C^T (C P_{n-1} C^T + Sigma)^-1, scaling the correction from prediction error
sequential Monte Carlo from sampling-importance-resampling; also bootstrap filter, survival of the fittest, condensation algorithm
